p: Relay lived in the basement of the Fort Collins data center, in a room that had been a storage closet until 2010. Marcus Bell had moved into it then and never left. Three monitors, a space heater he wasn't supposed to have, a coffee maker he definitely wasn't supposed to have, and a whiteboard covered in boxes and arrows that nobody else in the building could read.

Maria came down at 8:15 on Tuesday, straight from her one-on-one with Ochoa. He'd read her status page and asked one question. Do you know why yet? She'd said Marcus did. Ochoa had said, Then go find out what he knows. All of it. Write it down this time.

Marcus didn't look up when she knocked. He was a big man in a fleece vest, gray at the temples, twenty-two years into a career of making systems talk to each other that had never been built to. He'd written most of Relay himself, one interface at a time, and he kept the rest of it in his head.
Sit, he said, and pointed at a folding chair. This takes a minute. It's two problems. The first one is the boring one, and it's the one everybody's going to want to talk about.
On the middle monitor was a diagram she half recognized. A box for Relay. A line to Laramie. A smaller box on the line marked Cheyenne firewall, and someone had circled it in red, twice.

Plumbing, Marcus said. Everybody thinks the EHR is the hospital. It's not. It's a bunch of systems that don't know each other, and Relay is the pipes in the walls. You don't think about pipes until the ceiling's wet.
Maria pulled the chair up. For the next two months, she'd think about almost nothing else.

Marcus walked her through it the way he'd walk a new nurse through a drip. Relay held one open connection to MedaLink at Laramie, across the Wyoming network, through a firewall in Cheyenne. That connection had stayed open, day and night, for nine years.

Two Thursdays ago the change board approved a firewall cleanup. Listed as no clinical impact. One line in it cut the idle timeout from eight hours to sixty minutes. Laramie's lab goes quiet some nights between seven and eight. At 8:28 the firewall decided my connection was dead and dropped it. Didn't tell anybody. Relay kept sending into it, waiting for an ACK that was never coming. And I'd set it to wait forever, because in 2017 forever seemed safe.
He tapped the log. The emergency change note had my timestamps, so the firewall team found their side in ten minutes. That part went right.

Marcus sets an ACK timeout of thirty seconds, an automatic reconnect, and a heartbeat message every five minutes. The network team adds every Relay connection to the list the change board checks before approving any firewall work. Marcus tests it by having the network team drop the Laramie session on purpose. Relay reconnects in forty seconds and files a note saying it did.

Now the one you came for. Marcus opened his email. Relay had sent an alert at 8:41 PM, thirteen minutes after the connection died. Queue depth over threshold, Laramie lab results. It had gone to exactly one person.

It sat in a folder called Relay noise. The folder held 31,412 unread messages. Marcus scrolled for a long time to show her. Thresholds were set in 2015, when we had half the traffic. It fires forty times a day for nothing. So I filtered it. Everybody filters it. That's the part I wanted you sitting down for.

That afternoon Tasha Greene, the service desk manager, sent two more things without being asked. Two tickets from Laramie nurses, 9:10 PM and 10:02 PM. Labs slow? Logged as application slowness, low priority, closed the next morning as resolved.
Relay queue depth, Laramie lab results, the night of the outage. Messages waiting in the queue. Nothing moved from 8:28 PM until the restart at 11:56. The queue was empty by 12:30.

Marcus and Tasha rebuild the alerts around what nurses feel: the age of the oldest message and whether ACKs are coming back. Alerts page the service desk, which works around the clock, and the desk has a one-page runbook and an on-call engineer to call. Tasha links any ticket that says labs slow to interface status. They test it at 2 PM on a Wednesday by pausing a test feed. The desk calls Marcus in six minutes.

The patient safety review met Friday in a Laramie conference room with a speakerphone in the middle of the table. Fourteen people, among them the patient safety officer, the lab, the house supervisor, two nurse managers, a network engineer, Marcus, and Maria.
Maria walked through the night. The firewall change. The connection that waited forever. The alert at 8:41. The folder.
The Laramie quality director looked up from her notes. So the alert worked. It went to one person, and he didn't read it.
Every head in the room turned to Marcus. He looked at the table.

The alert went where we built it to go. One inbox, no on-call path, thresholds from 2015. That's mine. Then she lists the rest: a firewall change approved without a dependency check, an engine that waited forever, two nurse tickets triaged as slowness. The patient safety officer writes all four on the board. Marcus looks up for the first time.
The next Wednesday Nate Ostrowski, the CISO, sent Maria a list. His team had pulled every account with administrator rights on Relay. There were nine.

Marcus. Two consultants who'd left in 2019 and 2022. Four service accounts nobody could name an owner for. A shared account called relayadmin whose password, Nate wrote, was apparently known to four people and taped inside one drawer. And Maria Santos, granted for the Penwright interfaces during the build, never removed.
Nate had added one line under hers. Not used in ninety days. That's good. It's also why it shouldn't exist.

She writes back in two lines: remove mine today, and let's do the rest together. The consultants' accounts go first. The shared account takes three weeks, because Marcus's scripts use it, and each script gets its own service account with only the rights it needs. Nate replies with one word. Appreciated.
The new alerts took real work for each feed, and Marcus could do about twenty a month. Relay carried 214 interfaces.

Kiran printed the list and spread it across Maria's table. It read like a map of the whole health system. Registration's ADT feed out to the lab, pharmacy, radiology, dietary, and billing. Orders out, results back. Pharmacy to the dispensing cabinets. Images from PACS. Charges to the billing system. Census and ADT to Lumen, the discharge forecasting tool. The HIE. The portal. Two state reports. A feed to a dietary system that, as far as anyone could tell, had been turned off in 2020 and was still sending.
Twenty a month means eleven months, Kiran said. Where do you want to start?

They score every interface on one question: if this stops for three hours, what happens to a patient? Results, orders, ADT, and pharmacy land on top. Lumen and the billing feeds land in the middle, which revenue cycle grumbles about and accepts. Each application owner signs their row. The dietary feed gets turned off for real.

The Laramie backlog had filed, nearly 2,500 messages of it. Thirty-seven had come back from MedaLink with an error ACK. Marcus forwarded the reason, along with a message he'd translated into plain words for her.

One ADT message, in plain words. Message type A03, a discharge. Sent by registration at Laramie, 9:47 PM. Patient identification: medical record number 4 4 7 1 9 0 2. Visit: account number 8 8 1 3 0 4 5 5, medical surgical unit, room 214. Discharge date and time: 9:45 PM. Disposition: home.

Patients had been discharged while their results sat in the queue. When those results finally arrived, MedaLink refused to file them on visits that were already closed. Thirty-seven lab results, some normal, a few not, belonged to patients who were already home.

HIM confirms each patient against the master patient index and files each result to its own account number. The lab flags the six abnormal values. Kiran sends each discharging physician a list of their patients' late results. One gets a phone call the same night about a hemoglobin of 6.9.

Aisha Rahman caught Maria after the Clinical Informatics Council the second week of December. I want lactate times across all eleven hospitals. Order to result. I'm building something for sepsis and I need a baseline.

The eight Corvane hospitals sent lactate with a LOINC code. The three MedaLink hospitals sent it as LACT, LA2, or LACTWB, depending on the hospital and the year someone built it. Laramie had nine hundred local lab codes in all.
Kiran was already nodding. I can map all nine hundred. Weekends, maybe a month. It's fine. He said it the way he said yes to everything, before anyone had finished asking.

The Laramie lab director assigns a medical technologist to own the map. Kiran builds it in Relay, a hundred codes a week, and the lab validates each batch against real specimens. Lactate is done first. Aisha gets her baseline in January, and every code the lab signs is one less to fix at One Chart.
The Laramie ICU nurse manager called Maria directly. She'd been reviewing a rapid response from the week before, and the timeline didn't make sense.

The monitor says his pressure dropped at 3:14. My nurse called the team at 3:09. She didn't call them before it happened. The vitals in MedaLink are seven minutes off, and I think they've been off for a while.

Marcus found it by the end of the day. The bedside monitors sent vitals through a device gateway, and the gateway stamped them with its own clock. The gateway set its clock from a time server that had been retired in 2023. It had been drifting ever since.

Clinical engineering and the network team point the gateway, the monitors, and the pumps at Cascade's time service. They check other Wyoming device gateways and find one more. Then they trigger a test alarm at a set minute and confirm it files at that minute in MedaLink. The nurse manager gets a written note that her nurse called on time.

The call came from a pharmacist at Cheyenne, three days before Christmas. A patient transferred from Rawlins had arrived with twenty medications on the transfer summary. His wife had brought a paper list from home. It had twenty-three.

Marcus found it in an hour. MedaLink's continuity of care document export had a limit of twenty rows in the medication section, set in a 2012 build. Anything past twenty was dropped. The document didn't say it was cut short. It just ended.
Maria read the email twice. Then she sat back in her chair and looked at nothing for a while.
She'd held a medication list with a page missing once. Greeley, her first year, a transfer from a small hospital in Wyoming. She didn't tell Marcus the rest. She didn't really tell herself.

She files a safety event that afternoon. Until the fix, nurses sending a transfer from any MedaLink hospital call the receiving pharmacist when a patient has more than twenty medications. Kiran pulls every transfer from the last two years: forty-one patients had more than twenty. Pharmacy reviews each one. Marcus has the template fixed in eight days, with a line that says when a list is cut off, just in case.

The Laramie quality director wanted one more number for the safety review: lab turnaround time, order to result, for the whole month around the outage, by hour. The data warehouse team said it would be easy if they could connect straight to MedaLink's production database.
Read only, the warehouse lead said. After hours. We'll be careful.

Marcus, copied on the email, replied with a single line. Ask them what happened in March 2024. In March 2024 a report had run against MedaLink production at 2 PM and the nurses at Cheyenne couldn't chart for forty minutes.

The warehouse already loads MedaLink every night. The order and result times are there. The team builds the report from the copy in three days. Marcus sends Maria a thumbs up, which from Marcus is a speech.
Relay needed a patch, the first in two years. The change board approved a two hour window for the night of December 29. Every queue would hold during the window and drain after.

The Wyoming revenue cycle director called Maria the day before. It's year end. Every lab and pharmacy charge has to drop before the thirty-first, or it's next year's money and a mess for the auditors. Can the charge feeds go first when you come back up?
She wasn't wrong about the money. Glenn Morrow, the CFO, would care about year end too.

The window runs 1 to 3 AM. ADT, orders, results, and pharmacy drain first, then charges, which finish by 3:40. Revenue cycle runs a count against the lab and pharmacy systems the next morning. Every charge is there once. The director sends Maria a note: Easiest year end I've had.

Marcus was taking a week off after New Year's, his first in three years. His daughter was having a baby in Tucson. He came to Maria's office the afternoon of December 30 with a list of things that could go wrong while he was gone. It ran two pages, in pencil.
He set it on her desk and sat down without being asked, which was new. You stood up for the design in Laramie. Figured I owed you a list.
Maria had two junior analysts who'd asked to learn Relay. She'd asked Marcus twice. He'd changed the subject twice. This time she asked why.
He was quiet a long time. 2009. Hospital in Omaha. They asked me to write everything down. I did. Good binder. Three months later they handed the binder to a contractor and handed me a box.

She writes it into his role that afternoon: lead interface engineer, responsible for building the team's competency. The analysts will watch him, then work while he watches, then work alone, with a sign-off for each skill. He'll write the runbooks with them, not for them. Marcus reads it, then reads the last line again. This in my file? She says it is. He folds it into his vest pocket.

The patient safety review closed on the Tuesday between Christmas and New Year's. Four causes, four owners, eleven actions, and every one of them with a date. Ochoa read the final report at their one-on-one and set it down without a question, which Maria was learning was his highest compliment.
Two months ago you'd have fixed the interface, he said. This time you fixed the building it lives in. Keep doing that. It's slower and it's the job.
Marcus flew to Tucson on New Year's Day. That night he sent her a photo of the whiteboard in the basement, all of Relay's boxes and arrows, and nothing else.
Lucia was on the couch when she got home, a practice question for her nursing school interview open on her phone. What's a med rec?
Medication reconciliation. When a patient moves, somebody checks the list they came with against the list they're supposed to be on.
It is, Maria said. Until the list is short. Lucia looked up at her, waiting for the rest. Maria went to start dinner instead.

It had been a long two months, and most of it had gone right. The ceiling was dry. She knew where the pipes ran now, and who knew them, and that the answer to who knew them couldn't be one man in a fleece vest. She had a plan for that.
Two emails came in on Monday, January 4, three minutes apart.

The first was from Aisha Rahman. The lactate baseline is ugly. Sepsis is killing people in Wyoming slower than it should, but it's killing them. I want a sepsis alert live in all eleven hospitals by spring. I'm bringing it to the council next week. I'd like you to co-sponsor.
The second was from the Laramie medical staff office. It had an attachment.

Formal complaint, medical staff office. Submitted by Walter Hagen, MD, General Surgery, Laramie. Subject: click counts. Since changes made in December after the lab interface outage, a routine discharge now takes forty-seven clicks in MedaLink, up from forty-one. I was told the new system would be better. I would like it noted that the old one just got worse.
Maria sat with them both until her coffee went cold. Then she opened her calendar and blocked a week in Wyoming, on the floor, in scrubs.
